title: Nvidia Forecasts 70% Revenue Growth for Fiscal 2028 as AI Demand Accelerates
excerpt: The chipmaker reported $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue, more than double the year-ago period, and issued a rare forward-year guidance that far exceeded Wall Street projections.
body:
• Quarterly revenue hit $96.2 billion, more than doubling year-over-year, with data center sales reaching $89 billion
  • Nvidia forecast 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, far exceeding analyst expectations of roughly 44%
  • Next-generation Vera Rubin chips are shipping and will account for about one-fifth of data center revenue this quarter
  • Rising memory costs are expected to push gross margins down to 71-72% by Q4, from 74% in Q3

Nvidia on Wednesday reported quarterly revenue that more than doubled from a year ago and issued a rare forward-year forecast of 70% revenue growth, arguing that the AI computing boom is expanding rather than peaking.

The chipmaker posted $96.2 billion in revenue for the fiscal second quarter ended July 26, beating analyst estimates of $92.2 billion, according to LSEG data. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.22 per share, above the $2.10 consensus. Net income rose 126% to $59.7 billion.

"AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue."

— Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO

A Rare Year-Ahead Forecast

In an unusual move, Nvidia projected approximately 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, which ends in January 2028. Wall Street had expected growth of about 44%, according to Bloomberg data.

"We've never forecast or never guided to a year in advance," Huang said on the earnings call. The disclosure sent shares up nearly 5% in extended trading, reversing an initial 1% dip that followed the earnings release. Nvidia's market capitalization stands at approximately $5.1 trillion.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress framed the outlook as demand-driven. "Incredibly, we are seeing demand acceleration even at our scale," she said. "Customers' forecasts point to our growth doubling next year. However, we are supply-constrained."

Data Center Revenue Doubles

Data center revenue, which accounts for the vast majority of Nvidia's business, reached $89 billion in the quarter — up 117% year-over-year and ahead of the $85.1 billion analyst estimate, according to LSEG.

The company's next-generation Vera Rubin platform, now in full production, has started shipping to customers and will account for about one-fifth of data center revenue in the current quarter ending October. "Vera Rubin, now in full production, was built to power exactly this moment," Huang said.

Nvidia also announced an expanded partnership with Amazon Web Services, which will deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia GPUs across its global infrastructure in 2027 and 2028 — building on a March agreement for 1 million GPUs. AI labs, including OpenAI, are expected to contribute roughly a quarter of Nvidia's overall business next year.

So-called neo-cloud companies like Nebius and CoreWeave are projected to exit 2026 with more than eight gigawatts in Nvidia GPU capacity, up from three gigawatts at end of last year, according to the company.

Margins Under Pressure

Despite the revenue beats, rising costs are squeezing profitability. Soaring memory prices and higher component costs will push gross margins down to roughly 71-72% in the fiscal fourth quarter, down from about 74% in Q3, Kress said. Analysts had expected third-quarter margins of nearly 75%.

For the current quarter, Nvidia guided revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with analyst estimates of about $104.2 billion, according to LSEG.

China Sales Remain Uncertain

Nvidia's China business remains a wild card. Washington in May cleared roughly 10 Chinese firms — including Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance — to purchase Nvidia's H200 AI chip, but deliveries have been slow. A U.S. Commerce Department official said last month that shipments had begun but remained "very few." Nvidia did not include China data center revenue in its outlook.

What's Next

The results are likely to reinforce investor conviction that AI infrastructure spending has staying power beyond the current cycle. Huang pointed to a broadening customer base as evidence that demand is durable.

"This time last year, one lab alone was driving the build-out; today, we have a golden age of new AI labs and start-ups, multiple frontier labs scaling in parallel, a thriving open-model ecosystem and physical AI coming online," Huang said.
